title: How a career criminal fooled the system
article: Daniel Lamer started shooting people at 17. He has escaped jail three times, once wounding a guard, and another time taking a police officer hostage for 15 hours only to shoot him twice with the hopes that a "trophy killing" would earn him a place within the ranks of the bikers he admired.
"The pig .... I shot him twice," he screamed, running for cover.
In the end, the officer survived and the fugitive was condemned to prison for 20 years in 1991.
During the nine years he spent in jail for his crime, the Citizen has learned the career criminal acted as an assistant to the leader of a prison drug network controlled by the Hells Angels.

Still, the parole board figured it could take a chance on him. They noted his "genuine" remorse and believed his story that he'd give up crime for the life of an honest mechanic. After all, a prison psychologist said the inmate's "will and energy" could lead him to do "interesting things" in the community.

Mr. Lamer must have taken them for fools. After winning day parole in 2000, the 37-year-old Montrealer quit his garage job, and quickly reunited with members of a Hells Angels puppet gang, breaking his parole and resuming his path to prove himself worthy of membership.

And on Sunday morning, after he and an associate, Marc Bouffard, were pulled over on Highway 401 for speeding, Mr. Lamer stepped out of the car and opened fire on police. What exactly happened in the gunfight that left him dead on the side of the road has remained unclear until now.
It was just after 10 a.m., and a patrolling OPP officer spotted a speeding red Pontiac Sunfire with a Quebec licence plate headed west on the 401, near Morrisburg.

Armed and wearing bulletproof vests, the men were driving an economy-sized car to evade attention while taking care of business in Ontario on orders from senior bikers in Montreal. And now the police were in their way.
The driver, Marc Bouffard, is linked to The Rockers, a puppet gang used as enforcers for the Quebec Hells Angels Nomads chapter.
As they passed the Upper Canada Road exit, the officer activated his emergency lights and headed off in pursuit of the Pontiac, bringing it to a stop on a straight stretch of highway.

Then, the officer approached the driver's side of the vehicle and asked for Mr. Bouffard's driver's licence. Both the driver and passenger acted like they didn't speak a word of English. The officer then asked the driver to follow him back to the cruiser and showed him the back seat while he called for a bilingual officer to help.
Minutes later, Const. Dan Brisson pulled up his cruiser and so did another officer, accompanied by an auxiliary member.

Up ahead in the Pontiac, Daniel Lamer sat waiting in the passenger seat, revolver in hand. For a man who had escaped custody three times, going back to prison was not an option. To the bikers he admired, this would be his final chance to prove himself.
Minutes later, while two officers were talking to Mr. Bouffard, Mr. Lamer stepped out of the passenger's side.

It was Const. Brisson who spotted him first. The officer had started making his way over the car when Mr. Lamer suddenly turned around, drew a gun and opened fire on the police. He fired eight rounds.

All four officers ducked for cover, and as Const. Brisson turned back to duck behind a cruiser, he was hit in the back, the bullet ricocheting off his bullet-proof vest and grazing the back of his neck.
The constable never had the chance to return fire.

At this moment, another officer fired back, hitting the gunman at least five times -- in the right temple, neck and knee. At least two other rounds hit Mr. Lamer in the chest, but ricocheted off his bullet-proof vest.

Mr. Lamer fell to the ground and the officers raced to his side, and handcuffed him for fear he was still alive. Yesterday, Const. Brisson, who suffered only a minor wound, appeared shaken but otherwise not hurt.
For a man who made a career out of it, Mr. Lamer was bad at being a criminal. No matter how simple an escape or robbery, it always seemed to end in bullets-flying violence for him.
Take the last time he was on the run for breaking parole.

In May 1991, Mr. Lamer and another man held up a Montreal pharmacy for $68. A responding officer, Const. Richard Frohlich, chased the bandits into a tavern. Inside, they managed to disarm and handcuff the officer, dragging him into a stolen getaway car.
A pursuing officer shot out the car's rear tire and it crashed into a parked car in a residential neighbourhood. The men shuffled their hostage into a nearby home.

The homeowners had just sat down for supper when they heard someone banging at the door. A woman managed to run out the back door, but her husband wasn't quick enough and the men tied his wrists with electrical wire.

The armed bandits negotiated with police into the night --at one point securing a pack of cigarettes. They also spoke to their girlfriends on the phone and to one of their mothers, trying to calm them down after she learned of the standoff on the 11 o'clock news.
The next morning, the men decided to wash their clothes, saying they were starting to smell bad.
Mr. Lamer went for a shower, taking his revolver with him. And his associate fell asleep.

At this time, the officer slipped a hand out the handcuffs and jumped for his sleeping captor's gun. The officer ran to the shower and shooting started. The officer apparently emptied the gun, then ran into the living room and took cover behind the television set.
Naked and dripping wet, Mr. Lamer emerged from the bathroom, bleeding from a chest wound. He shot the officer twice, wounding him in the shoulder and thigh.
"The pig ... I shot him twice," he screamed.
The officer managed to jump through the living room window to safety and minutes later, the captors tossed their guns out the window and surrendered.
It would be 11 years until Mr. Lamer's next gunfight with police.
And his last.
